claims.text: The median cross-sectional correlation between adolescent social media use and life satisfaction across all operationalizations was small and negative (psi = -0.13).
The median longitudinal within-person effect of social media use on life satisfaction was trivial in size (beta = -0.05).
The median longitudinal within-person effect of life satisfaction on social media use was trivial in size (beta = -0.02).
Only 16% of significant specification curve models examining social media use and life satisfaction arose from male participant data.
In focused best-practice models for males, social media use predicted tenuous decreases only in satisfaction with life and in mean satisfaction (beta = -0.07 to -0.05).
In focused best-practice models for females, social media use predicted slightly decreased life satisfaction across all domains except satisfaction with appearance (beta = -0.09 to -0.04).
In focused best-practice models for females, all domains of life satisfaction except satisfaction with friends predicted slightly reduced social media use (beta = -0.11 to -0.07).

evidence.description: Across all operationalizations, the median cross-sectional correlation was negative (ψ = −0.13), an effect judged as small by behavioral scientists.
Both median longitudinal effects were trivial in size (social media predicting life satisfaction, β = −0.05).
Both median longitudinal effects were trivial in size (life satisfaction predicting social media use, β = −0.02).
When examining the range of possible specifications, the importance of gender was apparent: Only 16% of significant models arose from male data.

males showed only two longitudinal within-person effects: Social media predicted tenuous decreases in satisfaction with life and in mean satisfaction ( b = −0.08 to −0.04 or β = −0.07 to −0.05; Fig. 2 , Center ).

For females, however, social media was a predictor of slightly decreased life satisfaction across all domains, except satisfaction with appearance ( b = −0.13 to −0.05 or β = −0.09 to −0.04; Fig. 2 , Center ).
Furthermore, all domains of life satisfaction, except satisfaction with friends, predicted slightly reduced social media use ( b = −0.17 to −0.05 or β = −0.11 to −0.07; Fig. 2 , Right ).

methodologies.name: Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model specification curve analysis
methodologies.description: Combines random-intercept cross-lagged panel modeling with a specification curve analysis framework to evaluate between-person associations and within-person longitudinal effects across 2,268 distinct analysis options.
datasets: Understanding Society, the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009–2016)
conditions: Adolescents aged 10-15 years (n = 539 to 5,492 depending on analysis)
Weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted estimators
Predictive mean matching for missing data imputation
Four-wave completion threshold for participant inclusion

limitations.text: The yearly interval between measurements in the dataset might not be optimal for understanding reciprocal social media effects over time.
Self-report measures only partially reflect the objective time adolescents spend engaging with social media.

Prior research predominantly relies on cross-sectional associations between social media use and youth outcomes, making it impossible to separate longitudinal within-person effects from statistical artifacts.

future_work.text: Further exploration and replication of small reciprocal within-person effects in female adolescents.
Social media companies sharing granular user engagement data and participating in large-scale team-based open science to support independent research.
